Understanding structured concurrency

Structured concurrency means a child task cannot outlive the scope that created it. The lifetime of the work is visible in the shape of the code, which is the whole argument for it.

Consider a function that loads three resources concurrently. The straightforward version creates three tasks and awaits them in order, which is sequential in all but name:

let a = loadA()
let b = loadB()
let c = loadC()
return (a, b, c)

A task group says the same thing and enforces it. The group is the scope: when it exits, every child it started has finished or been cancelled, and there is no way to leak one past the closing brace.

await withTaskGroup(of: Value.self) { group in
	for loader in loaders {
		group.addTask { await loader() }
	}
	var results: [Value] = []
	for await value in group { results.append(value) }
	return results
}

The difference matters most under failure. If one child throws, the group cancels the rest and rethrows, so a partial result never escapes and a cancelled scope never leaves orphaned work running.

ConstructWaits forOn error
async leta fixed setrethrows at the await
Task groupa dynamic setcancels siblings

There is a cost. A group allocates, an async let does not, and for a handful of independent calls the simpler form reads better. Reach for the group when the set is dynamic or when the failure semantics matter.
